Jean Piaget. A Swiss psychologist and the founder of developmental psychology, whose theories of how children's minds grow and develop fundamentally changed education and our understanding of childhood itself. Unlike earlier views that children were simply miniature adults or passive recipients of knowledge waiting to be filled, Piaget proposed that children actively construct their understanding of the world through interaction and play, progressing through distinct stages with qualitatively different cognitive abilities at each level.

Born in Neuchâtel, Switzerland, Piaget began as a biologist before turning to psychology after becoming fascinated by how children reasoned and what their mistakes revealed about their thinking. In 1955, he founded the International Center for Genetic Epistemology in Geneva, where he spent decades conducting detailed observations of children solving problems and thinking through challenges. He conducted thousands of informal experiments, often using his own three children as subjects—not always by modern ethical standards, but with genuine curiosity and profound insight into how young minds work.

Piaget mapped out four stages of cognitive development. In the sensorimotor stage, from birth to two years, infants learn through sensation and movement and gradually develop object permanence, the understanding that objects exist even when out of sight, a major cognitive achievement. The preoperational stage, from two to seven years, sees children thinking with symbols and language, but they're egocentric, unable to take another's perspective, and they fail conservation tasks—they believe that quantity changes when shape does. In the concrete operational stage, from seven to eleven years, children can perform logical operations on concrete objects and understand conservation. They begin to decentrate, focusing on multiple features at once rather than just one obvious dimension. Finally, in the formal operational stage, beginning around twelve, adolescents and adults can reason abstractly, hypothetically, and systematically. They can think about thinking, imagine hypothetical scenarios, and reason with variables.

Central to Piaget's theory are several key concepts. A schema is a mental structure or framework for understanding the world that develops and becomes more complex with experience. Assimilation is the process of incorporating new information into existing schemas. Accommodation is modifying those schemas when new information doesn't fit existing structures. Constructivism is the epistemological principle that knowledge is not passively absorbed but actively constructed by the learner through interaction. Conservation is the crucial understanding that quantity remains constant despite changes in appearance—water poured into a different-shaped glass is still the same amount, a seemingly obvious fact that children don't understand at first.

Piaget's revolution was philosophical and practical. He elevated childhood from a preparatory stage to be endured into a fascinating realm of genuinely different but no less sophisticated thinking. This dignity and respect for children's minds reshaped education from rote memorization toward discovery, exploration, and problem-solving. His stages provided a framework that, while later refined, still anchors how educators and parents understand development today. The conservation task became iconic—a simple, elegant demonstration that children don't think like adults. Piaget also pioneered a method of careful observation and questioning that became standard in developmental psychology. Though his theories have been revised and his age ranges questioned, his core insight remains true: minds develop, mature, and transform qualitatively through childhood. Understanding how a child thinks—why they believe inanimate objects have feelings, why they struggle with multiple perspectives—opens pathways to better teaching, parenting, and raising emotionally attuned and intellectually capable humans.
